etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English schade, from Old English sċeadu, sċadu (“shadow; shade”), from Proto-West Germanic *skadu, from Proto-Germanic *skadwaz (“shadow; shade”). More at shadow.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) Darkness where light, particularly sunlight, is blocked.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter VIII, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: Now we plunged into a deep shade with the boughs lacing each other overhead, and crossed dainty, rustic bridges over the cold trout-streams, the boards giving back the clatter of our horses' feet: […] .

definitions.definition: (countable) Something that blocks light, particularly in a window.
(countable) A variety of a color, in particular one obtained by adding black (compare tint).

quote.citation: 1689 (indicated as 1690), [John Locke], An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding. […], London:  […]  Eliz[abeth] Holt, for Thomas Basset, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Thus light and colours, as white, red, yellow, blue, with their several degrees or shades, and mixtures, as green, scarlet, purple, sea-green, and the rest, come in only by the eyes […]

definitions.definition: (figuratively) A subtle variation in a concept.

quote.citation: 1823, Thomas De Quincey, Letters to a Young Man whose Education has been Neglected. No. V. On the English Notices of Kant:
quote.text: new shades and combinations of thought

quote.citation: 1849–1861, Thomas Babington Macaulay, chapter III, in The History of England from the Accession of James the Second, volume (please specify |volume=I to V), London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, →OCLC:
quote.text: Every shade of religious and political opinion had its own headquarters.

definitions.definition: (figuratively) An aspect that is reminiscent of something.
A very small degree of a quantity, or variety of meaning

quote.citation: 1934, Agatha Christie, Miss Marple Tells a Story:
quote.text: Mrs. Rhodes who (so I gathered from Mr. Petherick's careful language) was perhaps just a shade of a hypochondriac, had retired to bed immediately after dinner.

quote.citation: 1990 April 7, Wickie Stamps, “The 'Temple' Is Familiar”, in Gay Community News, page 12:
quote.text: Five feet in diameter and a shade above knee high, the center of the fragile white canvass structure is filled with  […]

definitions.definition: (chiefly literary and fantasy) A ghost or specter; a spirit.

quote.citation: 1700, [John] Dryden, “Ceyx and Alcyone”, in Fables Ancient and Modern; […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Swift as thought the flitting shade / Thro' air his momentary journey made.

quote.citation: 1956, Anthony Burgess, Time for a Tiger (The Malayan Trilogy), published 1972, page 39:
quote.text: Still, Birch House (a sop to the shade of the murdered Perak Resident) had no more than its normal share of flagellation[.]

definitions.definition: (countable) A postage stamp showing an obvious difference in colour/color to the original printing and needing a separate catalogue/catalog entry.
(uncountable, originally LGBTQ slang) Subtle insults.

quote.citation: 1990, Jennie Livingston, director, Paris Is Burning, spoken by Dorian Corey:
quote.text: Shade is: "I don't tell you you're ugly, but I don't have to tell you because you know you're ugly." And that's shade.

definitions.definition: (countable) A cover around or above a light bulb, a lampshade.

quote.citation: 1979 August, Graham Burtenshaw, Michael S. Welch, “O.V.S. Bulleid's SR loco-hauled coaches - 1”, in Railway World, page 398:
quote.text: Lighting was unimaginative for the standard stock with naked tungsten filament bulbs and metal reflectors. However, all compartments had individual reading lights above the seats with attractive glass shades.

definitions.definition: (historical) A candle-shade.

quote.text: I am now finishing this letter by candle-light, with the help of a handkerchief tied over the shade.

His tent is furnished with a good large bed, mattress, pillow, &c., a few camp-stools or chairs, a folding table, a pair of shades for his candles, six or seven trunks with table equipage, his stock of linen (at least 24 shirts); some dozens of wine, brandy, and gin; tea, sugar, and biscuit; and a hamper of live poultry and his milch-goat.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English schaden, from the noun.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To shield (someone or something) from light.
(intransitive, rare) To shield oneself from light.
(transitive) To alter slightly.
(intransitive) To vary or approach something slightly, particularly in color.

quote.citation: 1886, Edmund Gurney, Phantasms of the Living:
quote.text: This small group will be most conveniently treated with the emotional division, into which it shades.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, baseball, of a defensive player) To move slightly from one's normal fielding position.
(transitive) To darken, particularly in drawing.
To win by a narrow margin.

quote.citation: 2024 March 10, David Hytner, “Doku involved at both ends as Liverpool and Manchester City share spoils”, in The Guardian‎[1]:
quote.text: It was Alexis Mac Allister who lit the touchpaper at the start of the second half, scoring from the penalty spot to cancel out John Stones’s opener for City midway through a first half that the defending champions had shaded.

definitions.definition: (transitive, graphical user interface) To reduce (a window) so that only its title bar is visible.
(transitive, slang) To throw shade, to subtly insult someone.

quote.citation: 2021 December 8, Arwa Mahdawi, “Elon Musk is learning a hard lesson: never date a musician”, in The Guardian‎[2]:
quote.text: The lyrics have prompted headlines about her “shading” Musk with a “spicy dig”, but I reckon the guy got off lightly.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To shelter; to cover from injury; to protect; to screen.

quote.citation: c. 1608–1609 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Coriolanus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i]:
quote.text: Ere in our own house I do shade my head.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To present a shadow or image of; to shadow forth; to represent.

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book V, Canto VII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], part II (books IV–VI), London:  […]  [Richard Field] for William Ponsonby, →OCLC, stanza 3, page 268:
quote.text: His [Osiris’s] wife was Iſis, whom they likewiſe made / A Goddeſſe of great powre and ſouerainty, / And in her perſon cunningly did ſhade / That part of Iuſtice, which is Equity,  […]
